StringWithMarkup.String: Laboratory studies in a 14 day toxicity test of the formulated preparations of 8 fungicides (benomyl, bupirimat, captafopl, captan, Cu-oxychloride, fentin acetate + maneb, folpet, triadimefon), 5 herbicides (atrazine, calcium cynamide, monolinuron, paraquat, sodium chlorate), a plant regulator (chlormequat chloride) and 10 insecticides (aldicarb, carbofuran, dialifos, endosulfan, lindane, methamidophos, methidathion, propoxur, terbufos, triazophos) were performed on 2 species of earthworms, Lumbricus terrestris and Eisenia foetida. LC50 values were determined for the pesticides homogeneously incorporated into the test soil substrates in aqueous suspension or by grinding in a portion of quartz sand. Despite the diverse chemical structures of the compounds tested, there was species specificity in the earthworm toxicity of different pesticides. There was also a difference in the sensitivity of worms of the same species to different pesticides. Behavioral disturbances of earthworms caused by the insecticides were more severe than those caused by fungicides or herbicides. The loss in live weight (biomass) of earthworms was independent of the lethal effect of the compound and, in addition to the mortality values, was considered an important criterium for the determination of the sublethal effects. The lethal effects on earthworms are discussed to show the value of the toxicity tests in the hazard evaluation of pesticides on beneficial soil organisms.

StringWithMarkup.String: Monolinuron's production and use as a herbicide will result in its release to the environment through its use and from various waste streams. If released to soil, monolinuron should have medium mobility based on an average experimental value for Koc of 271.5. Volatilization of monolinuron is not expected to be important from moist or dry surfaces given an estimated Henry's Law constant of 4.6X10-8 atm-cu m/mole and an experimental vapor pressure of 1.5X10-4 mm Hg. Half-lives for monolinuron in soil have been determined to be 60 days and 33-66 days. Photolysis of monolinuron should occur on soil surfaces according to its degradation by light at wavelengths greater than 290 nm. According to a biodegradation study using a mixed bacterial culture, monolinuron is expected to biodegrade quickly in soil and water. If released to water, monolinuron may adsorb to suspended solids and sediment according to experimental Koc values of 40-2025. Monolinuron will be essentially non-volatile from water surfaces based on an estimated Henry's Law constant of 4.6X10-8 atm-cu m/mole. Experimental BCF values ranging from <20 to 140, suggest that monolinuron will undergo moderate to high bioconcentration in aquatic organisms. The half-life of monolinuron in water has been determined to be 22 days. If released to the atmosphere, monolinuron will exist as a vapor in the ambient atmosphere. Vapor-phase monolinuron is degraded in the atmosphere by reaction with photochemically produced hydroxyl radicals with an estimated half-life of about 27 hours. Particulate-phase monolinuron may be physically removed from the air by wet and dry deposition. (SRC)

Section.Description: Sorption to soils and sediments is an important factor on the transport and fate of organic contaminants in the environment.  The soil/water adsorption coefficient, also known as solid-water distribution coefficient (Kd), measures the amount of chemical substance adsorbed onto soil per amount of water.  Since adsorption occurs predominantly by partition into the soil organic matter, it is more useful to normalize the Kd value to the organic carbon content of a soil and express the distribution coefficient in Koc (organic carbon normalized distribution coefficient).  The greater the Kd (or Koc) value, the less likely a chemical will leach or contribute to runoff.  A very high value means it is strongly adsorbed onto soil and organic matter and does not move throughout the soil.
